"text": "八集剧集《造反派》（目前可在 arte 视频点播平台观看）在众多剧集作品中脱颖而出，因为它既不属于罪案剧，也不属于恐怖片。它包含许多喜剧元素，但本身并非喜剧。它致力于探讨某个历史事件，却又与战争、灾难及其他危机毫无关系。剧中确实出现了知名知识分子，但通常只有在极少数情况下，人们才会为他们拍摄一部虚构剧集。由本杰明·夏尔比（Benjamin article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In der arte-Mediathek kann man aktuell eine bemerkenswerte französische Serie entdecken. „Die Revoluzzer“ spielt im Jahr 1969 an der neugegründeten Universität Vincennes, die nach den Unruhen von 1968 die Lage beruhigen sollte. Die acht Folgen kreisen um Studierende und Lehrkräfte an der Uni und zeichnen sich durch den leichten Tonfall aus, mit dem sie das geschichtliche Thema behandeln. Einfallsreich sind auch der Einsatz von dokumentarischem Material und Anspielungen auf Filme der Nouvelle Vague."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die achtteilige Serie „ Die Revoluzzer “ (aktuell in der arte-Mediathek ) sticht aus den seriellen Produktionen heraus, denn sie lässt sich weder dem Krimi- noch dem Horror-Genre zuordnen. Sie besitzt viele komische Momente, ohne eine Komödie zu sein. Sie widmet sich einem historischen Ereignis, ohne dass sie etwas mit Krieg, Katastrophen und anderen Krisen zu tun hätte. In ihr kommen zwar prominente Intellektuelle vor, doch denen würde man nur im Ausnahmefall eine fiktionale Serie widmen. Der Mehrteiler von Benjamin Charbit und Dominique Baumard ist ein Unikum und spielt im Jahr 1969, als die Reform-Uni Vincennes gegründet wurde, die vieles anders machen sollte als die klassischen Hochschulen in Frankreich. Sie sollte sich beispielsweise Menschen öffnen, die wie die meisten Kinder von Arbeitern und Arbeitsemigranten sowie viele Frauen nicht den etablierten Ausbildungsweg genossen hatten.", "links": [{"text": "Die Revoluzzer", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/627142/die-revoluzzer"}, {"text": "arte-Mediathek", "url": "https://www.arte.tv/de/videos/RC-028039/die-revoluzzer/"}, {"text": "Benjamin Charbit", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/371537/benjamin-charbit"}, {"text": "Dominique Baumard", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/423766/dominique-baumard"}, {"text": "Vincennes", "url": "https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A4t_Paris_VIII"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/375234/die-revoluzzer-szenenbild-6.jpg?t=1787751866", "alt": "Proben mit Molotowcocktails: Lulja Comar & Manon Kneusé in „Die Revoluzzer“", "caption": "Proben mit Molotowcocktails: Lulja Comar & Manon Kneusé in „Die Revoluzzer“ (© Agat Films)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ihre Gründung war ein doppelter Reflex auf die Unruhen vom Mai 1968, als die Studentinnen und Studenten auf die Straße gingen und sich ihr Protest, den die Polizei niederzuknüppeln versuchte, zu einer gesellschaftlichen Krise auswuchs, die selbst Charles de Gaulle für kurze Zeit Schutz im benachbarten Deutschland suchen ließ. Vincennes sollte nicht nur Auswege aus der Bildungskrise finden, sondern zugleich die kritischen Intellektuellen von der Sorbonne im Zentrum von Paris abziehen und an die Peripherie versetzen, damit in der französischen Hauptstadt selbst wieder Ruhe einkehrte."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Das könnte Sie auch interessieren:"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Leders Journal (59): Die Gier ist ein Luder - Alexander Held", "links": [{"text": "Leders Journal (59): Die Gier ist ein Luder - Alexander Held", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/artikel/81450/alexander-held-und-munchner-mord"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Leders Journal (58): „Der verlorene Schlaf“ – ein cinephiler Lesetipp", "links": [{"text": "Leders Journal (58): „Der verlorene Schlaf“ – ein cinephiler Lesetipp", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/artikel/81114/leders-journal-58-der-verlorene-schlaf-lesetipp"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Leders Journal (57): Das Fernsehen und die Fußball-WM", "links": [{"text": "Leders Journal (57): Das Fernsehen und die Fußball-WM", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/artikel/80684/die-fussball-wm-2026-im-spiegel-der-medien"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dieses Konzept ging zunächst auf. Viele Revolutionäre – sowohl unter den Lehrenden wie den Studierenden – wechselten nach Vincennes, wo sie weniger studieren als über ihre Strategien nachdenken wollten. Als Gruppe waren sie zu diesem Zeitpunkt schon zerfallen. Die einen solidarisierten sich ein Jahr nach dem Einmarsch der Staaten des Warschauer Paktes immer noch mit der Sowjetunion und scharten sich um die Kommunistische Partei Frankreichs (KPF) und ihre einflussreiche Gewerkschaft CGT. article_text:
In der arte-Mediathek kann man aktuell eine bemerkenswerte französische Serie entdecken. „Die Revoluzzer“ spielt im Jahr 1969 an der neugegründeten Universität Vincennes, die nach den Unruhen von 1968 die Lage beruhigen sollte. Die acht Folgen kreisen um Studierende und Lehrkräfte an der Uni und zeichnen sich durch den leichten Tonfall aus, mit dem sie das geschichtliche Thema behandeln. Einfallsreich sind auch der Einsatz von dokumentarischem Material und Anspielungen auf Filme der Nouvelle Vague.

Die achtteilige Serie „ Die Revoluzzer “ (aktuell in der arte-Mediathek ) sticht aus den seriellen Produktionen heraus, denn sie lässt sich weder dem Krimi- noch dem Horror-Genre zuordnen. Sie besitzt viele komische Momente, ohne eine Komödie zu sein. Sie widmet sich einem historischen Ereignis, ohne dass sie etwas mit Krieg, Katastrophen und anderen Krisen zu tun hätte. In ihr kommen zwar prominente Intellektuelle vor, doch denen würde man nur im Ausnahmefall eine fiktionale Serie widmen. Der Mehrteiler von Benjamin Charbit und Dominique Baumard ist ein Unikum und spielt im Jahr 1969, als die Reform-Uni Vincennes gegründet wurde, die vieles anders machen sollte als die klassischen Hochschulen in Frankreich. Sie sollte sich beispielsweise Menschen öffnen, die wie die meisten Kinder von Arbeitern und Arbeitsemigranten sowie viele Frauen nicht den etablierten Ausbildungsweg genossen hatten.

Ihre Gründung war ein doppelter Reflex auf die Unruhen vom Mai 1968, als die Studentinnen und Studenten auf die Straße gingen und sich ihr Protest, den die Polizei niederzuknüppeln versuchte, zu einer gesellschaftlichen Krise auswuchs, die selbst Charles de Gaulle für kurze Zeit Schutz im benachbarten Deutschland suchen ließ. Vincennes sollte nicht nur Auswege aus der Bildungskrise finden, sondern zugleich die kritischen Intellektuellen von der Sorbonne im Zentrum von Paris abziehen und an die Peripherie versetzen, damit in der französischen Hauptstadt selbst wieder Ruhe einkehrte.

Leders Journal (58): „Der verlorene Schlaf“ – ein cinephiler Lesetipp

Dieses Konzept ging zunächst auf. Viele Revolutionäre – sowohl unter den Lehrenden wie den Studierenden – wechselten nach Vincennes, wo sie weniger studieren als über ihre Strategien nachdenken wollten. Als Gruppe waren sie zu diesem Zeitpunkt schon zerfallen. Die einen solidarisierten sich ein Jahr nach dem Einmarsch der Staaten des Warschauer Paktes immer noch mit der Sowjetunion und scharten sich um die Kommunistische Partei Frankreichs (KPF) und ihre einflussreiche Gewerkschaft CGT. Andere sahen im maoistischen China, dem ideologischen wie geopolitischen Konkurrenten der Sowjetunion, ihre politische Heilserwartung erfüllt. Hinzukamen Trotzkisten aller Schattierungen, die sich ideologisch an der Sowjetunion abarbeiteten, sowie Anarchisten, die alle kommunistischen Staaten als repressiv ablehnten und von einem Einfluss träumten, den ihre spanischen Genossen in den frühen 1930er-Jahren genossen hatten.

Theorie und Realität der Revolution

Vor diesem Hintergrund erzählt die Serie von dem, was in Vincennes etwa ein Jahr lang geschah. Allerdings stammen viele der realen Ereignisse, die durch Dokumentaraufnahmen in die fiktionale Geschichte der Serie eingewoben sind, aus späteren Jahren; selbst auf das Ende der Hochschule und den Abriss der Gebäude im Jahr 1980 wird bereits am Anfang verwiesen.

Erzählt wird das aus der Perspektive von mehreren Personen. Von Françoise Bardel ( Lulja Comar ), die als junge Frau aus der Provinz nach Vincennes kommt, um zu studieren und die kulturelle Revolte mitzuerleben, von der alle sprechen. Von Amadéo Moreira ( Micha Lescot ), einem Studenten, der politisch wie sexuell durch alle Lager und Konfessionen geistert und für überraschende Aktionen sorgt. Von Gérard Gérard ( Pierre-François Garel ), einem Professor, der über die Theorie der Revolution ein Buch geschrieben hat und nun plötzlich an seinen Taten gemessen wird. Und von André Merloux ( Grégory Gadebois ), dem Rektor der Universität, der nach anfänglichen Zweifeln selbst mit den wildesten Aktionen der Studentinnen und Studenten sympathisiert und die Reform-Universität gegenüber dem immer stärker zweifelnden Ministerium verteidigt.

Die ungewöhnlichste Figur ist die Prostituierte Claudine Biscarri ( Manon Kneusé ), die von ihrem Liebhaber, einem Agenten der politischen Polizei, als Spionin in die Hochschule geschickt wird, dort aber nicht nur einen starken Bewusstseinswandel durchmacht, sondern sich emanzipiert und dann sogar noch zu einer zentralen Figur des Widerstands gegen die Willkür des Staates aufsteigt.

Wer auf Stipendien angewiesen ist

Selbstverständlich trägt das Züge einer Kolportage, zu der sich Aufstiegs- und Liebesgeschichten, Betrügereien, Abhöraktionen, eine Entführung und Demonstrationen aller Art fügen. Das sorgt für die aus Serien gewohnte Abwechslung und zudem immer wieder für eine gewisse Spannung, selbst wenn das Ende der Hochschule ja schon früh vorweggenommen wird. Alle Figuren haben sympathische Momente, sodass man ihnen selbst den politischen Unsinn, den sie von sich geben, als Teil einer nachgeholten Pubertät verzeiht. Vielen politischen Aktionen ist eine gewisse Absurdität eigen, wenn etwa ein Streik dafür sorgt, dass die Studierenden, die auf Stipendien angewiesen sind, die notwendigen Prüfungen nicht ablegen können.

Politisch ist vieles, was die Serie anreißt oder benennt, aus heutiger Sicht durchaus problematisch, etwa wenn sich die Gruppe, die sich um Françoise bildet, maoistisch nennt. Denn in China wurden genau zu dieser Zeit Intellektuelle und Professoren, die in Vincennes hofiert wurden, von den Kulturrevolutionären durch die Straßen gejagt und als „Sozialschmarotzer“ denunziert. Auch die Widersprüche zwischen den Kadern der KPF und der CGT und allen anderen, die sich als Revolutionäre verstanden, dienen vor allem der Situationskomik, was an der Wut, die beiden Lager gegeneinander hegten, komplett vorbeigeht.

Dennoch schaut man dem bunten Treiben, das sich vor allem in der Kleidung mit Miniröcken, Jeans und Lederjacken sowie den wilden Frisuren spiegelt, gerne zu. Das hat auch damit zu tun, dass Dominique Baumard und Benjamin Charbit die fiktionale Geschichte mit einer gewissen Raffinesse immer wieder aus dokumentarischem Filmmaterial entwickeln. Das geht so weit, dass sie Ausschnitte aus einer Rede des Psychoanalytikers Jacques Lacan für ein fiktives Gespräch verwenden, in dem der Rektor, der nicht mehr weiterweiß, ihn um persönliche Hilfe bittet.

Raffiniertes Spiel mit Nouvelle-Vague-Zitaten

Noch wichtiger ist, dass manche Passage als Pastiche auf Filme der Nouvelle Vague angelegt ist, was durchaus legitim ist, da in Vincennes von Beginn an Filmwissenschaft gelehrt wurde und sich mancher Regisseur als Lehrender angeboten hatte. So finden sich liebevolle Anspielungen auf Chris Marker , was die Montage von historischem Material betrifft, auf Jean-Luc Godard , was viele Text- und Bildmontagen angeht, auf Agnès Varda und die Farbgestaltung ihrer Filme sowie vor allem auf Jacques Demy . Ihm wurde gleichsam eine ganze Folge gewidmet, in der Dialogpassagen gesungen werden. Genauso wie es Demy vorgemacht hatte, der selbst die Geschichte eines Streiks in „ Ein Zimmer in der Stadt “ (1982) in vielen Songs darstellte.

Arte verzichtet im Zusammenhang mit „Die Revoluzzer“ aktuell darauf, den Dokumentarfilm „ Vincennes - Die revolutionäre Uni “ zu wiederholen. Darin rekonstruiert Virginie Linhart die Geschichte der Reform-Universität in vielen Interviews und mit einem reichhaltigen Dokumentarmaterial. Der Film ist bei Youtube zu sehen, und wer ihn zum Vergleich hinzuzieht, wird verblüfft sein, dass vieles, was an der Serie besonders fiktiv erscheint, etwa die Geschichte der Prostituierten, im Dokumentarfilm als real geschildert wird. Das gilt auch für den Streik des Reinigungspersonals oder für die Entführung des Regisseurs; die Serie unterschlägt allerdings, dass sie für den Entführten nicht ganz so glimpflich wie geschildert verlief.

Manches aus „Die Revoluzzer“ relativiert sich: Viele Stars unter den Lehrenden waren nur kurze Zeit in Vincennes. So zog es Michel Foucault beispielsweise bald zum Collège de France in Paris. Vielsagend ist, dass die Serie zwei für die Reform-Universität entscheidende Dinge außer Acht lässt. Zum einen, dass die Gründer sich in vielen Dingen auf die USA bezogen; Vincennes wurde ausdrücklich als Campus-Uni wie Berkeley konzipiert und der Lehrbetrieb wie in vielen US-Colleges strukturiert. Obwohl in dieser Zeit die USA wegen des Vietnamkriegs als politischer Feind der Polit-Kader in Vincennes galten.

Zum anderen fehlt auch, dass diese Hochschule mit Medienapparaturen hochgerüstet wurde. Alle Seminarräume verfügten über Fernsehapparate und Telefone. In der Filmklasse wurde auf Film gedreht. Es gab ein eigenes professionelles Videosystem, mit dem Lehrveranstaltungen und Vollversammlungen aufgenommen und wiedergegeben wurden. Bei Vorlesungen der Prominenz stand eine Batterie von Mikrofonen und Tonbandgeräten vor ihnen. Zugleich gab es ein großes Interesse des Fernsehens an Vincennes. All das sorgte für eine enorme Menge an Archivmaterial, aus dem der Dokumentarfilm, aber auch die Serie reichlich zitieren.

Serie und Dokumentarfilm bieten zusammengenommen umfangreiches Material über einen Teil der Gesellschafts- und Mediengeschichte, die bis heute nachwirkt. Im gewalttätigen Protest gegen das Schulsystem, der derzeit in Frankreich wütet, spürt man dieselbe Faszination für die Gewalt, wie sie 1969 auch in Vincennes zu spüren war. Eine Wut, die sich schnell funktionalisieren ließ.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 馆长兼首席执行官丹尼尔·韦斯（Daniel Weiss）表示：“我们在教育方面没有太多专门的空间，因此一直有点像是临时凑合出来的。”

article_text:
The Philadelphia Museum of Art announced Friday that it has received one of the largest gifts in its history: $20 million from Comcast cofounder Julian A. Brodsky and his wife, Lois G. Brodsky. The gift will support the creation of a new education center named for the donors, vastly expanding on the museum’s existing education spaces.

The current education space clocks in at under 6,000 square feet; the new Brodsky Center will more than triple that area. The museum currently has just 16 education staffers, including both full- and part-time workers, and it plans to expand that cohort, which now serves about 36,000 students a year.

“We don’t have much in the way of dedicated space for education, so it’s been slightly improvisational,” director and CEO Daniel Weiss told ARTnews in a phone conversation. “Nonetheless, we have an active commitment to doing it. This gift will facilitate a higher level of commitment to the work and expand the number of people we can serve, and allow us to innovate new programs we don’t have now because we don’t have space. It’s an obvious thing for a comprehensive museum like ours to have, but we don’t have one.”

Weiss joined the museum last December after the board of trustees dismissed his predecessor ; in an ARTnews profile published this month, Hilarie M. Sheets wrote that he is “widely viewed as a smart and thoughtful straight shooter, skilled at solving organizational problems.” The museum had run a $10 million deficit for the 2025–26 fiscal year, on a $76.5 million budget.

The Brodsky gift will transform the museum’s north wing and is the first major capital undertaking since the Core Project, Frank Gehry’s four-year renovation and expansion, which opened to the public in 2021. Initial plans include a family learning center, art studios, a visitor orientation area, and a multipurpose community hub. The museum will work with Philadelphia architecture firm MGA Partners on the design, which is anticipated to be completed by summer 2027, with construction slated to be finished within a few years.

“Lois and I are incredibly happy to support the new Learning and Engagement Center,” said Julian Brodsky in press materials. “It comes at a wonderful moment, bringing together so many of the initiatives we are passionate about and reflecting our deep love for the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Throughout our lives, we have been ardently involved in educational initiatives, with a particular focus on children and families from underserved communities.”

The Brodskys are longtime supporters of the museum. He joined the board in 1995 and became an emeritus trustee in 2024, remaining vice chair of the library and archives committee. She began volunteering there in 1982 and serves on the committees for conservation, European art, and prints, drawings, and photographs. A gallery was named for them in 2005 in recognition of their support of the institution’s 125th anniversary campaign, and they endowed a photography curator position in 2009. Brodsky’s net worth has not been publicly disclosed; Comcast’s current market capitalization is over $81 billion.

“The new Brodsky Center will be an intentionally designed, purpose-built space that inspires limitless educational experiences grounded in the PMA’s collection,” said Audrey Hudson, the museum’s deputy director for learning and engagement, in press materials. “It will address the museum’s need for expanded capacity to host school groups, while providing dedicated spaces for programming and studios for hands-on learning.”

article_text:
Volker Schlöndorf begleitet den Start seines neuen Spielfilms „Heimsuchung - Eine Jahrhundertgeschichte“ und stellt die Literaturverfilmung nach dem Roman von Jenny Erpenbeck in zwölf deutschen Städten persönlich vor. Bei einigen Terminen sind auch die Produzentin Regina Ziegler und Jenny Erpenbeck als Autorin der Romanvorlage mit dabei.

Die Literaturkritik war überaus angetan, als Jenny Erpenbeck im Jahr 2007 ihren Roman „ Heimsuchung “ veröffentlichte. Auf nur knapp 200 Seiten blättert Erpenbeck ein ganzes Jahrhundert deutscher Geschichte auf, wobei der Schauplatz durchgängig ein Grundstück am Scharmützelsee bei Berlin ist. Zu dessen Bewohnern zählen unter anderem ein Architekt, ein jüdischer Tuchfabrikant und eine Schriftstellerin; dabei werden das frühe 20. Jahrhundert, die NS-Zeit, die DDR und die Nachwende thematisiert. Eine Adaption des Stoffes fürs Kino war nur eine Frage der Zeit, und auch der Regisseur lag durchaus nahe: Volker Schlöndorff gilt seit seinem Debüt „ Der junge Törless “ (1965) und gefeierten Filmen wie „ Die Blechtrommel “ (1978) sowohl als Spezialist für Literaturverfilmungen wie auch für historische Stoffe. Seine mit namhaften deutschen Schauspielern besetzte Verfilmung „ Heimsuchung - Eine Jahrhundertgeschichte “ feierte im Mai 2026 in Cannes Premiere.

Im Filmdienst hieß es zur Uraufführung: „Schlöndorff meistert die Adaption des literarisch fein gesponnenen Romans mit vertrauter Souveränität, indem er das Bilderbuchhafte einer werktreuen Adaption mehr und mehr hinter sich lässt und in den beiden Kapiteln um die NS- und DDR-Zeit einen eigenständigen Atem entfaltet. Darin spiegelt sich dann auch deutlicher der weibliche Blick auf die Zeitläufte, die mit dem fortschreitenden Jahrhundert von den Protagonistinnen zunehmend mehr mitgestaltet werden.“

Schlöndorff präsentiert seinen ersten Kinospielfilm seit 2017 flankierend zum Kinostart ab dem 6. Oktober persönlich in zwölf deutschen Städten. Im Anschluss an die jeweiligen Vorführungen steht der Regisseur für Filmgespräche zur Verfügung; in einigen Fällen sind auch die Produzentin Regina Ziegler und die Romanautorin Jenny Erpenbeck mit von der Partie.

Regulär startet „ Heimsuchung - Eine Jahrhundertgeschichte “ am 15. Oktober im Verleih von StudioCanal in den Kinos.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 1968年8月苏联军队入侵捷克斯洛伐克首都时，寇德卡是第一批到达现场的人之一。

"text": "一切皆出于偶然，这用来开启与一位摄影师的对话似乎有些奇怪——他的专注、强度、精准以及纯粹的意志体现在他存在的方方面面，更不用说他所承担过的每一个项目。然而，约瑟夫·寇德卡（Josef "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡始终保持着毫不松懈的警觉，“去抓住这些偶然的机会，因为它们可能是最具启示性的。”他以开放的心态和胸怀工作，凭借直觉知道阿瑟·米勒（Arthur Miller）曾经写下的何时“必须给予关注”。1968年8月21日，当布拉格遭到苏联主导的华沙条约组织坦克入侵时，他敏锐、近乎野兽般的直觉让他别无选择，只能立刻走上街头开始拍摄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "寇德卡是一位不带伤感情绪的摄影师，他以不带先入之见的态度、惊人的精力和人性投入工作，其自身本质似乎与对个人自由的渴望（看似已经得到满足）深深交织在一起。与这种在世界上充满活力的方式相一致的，是他对他人自由和个人主义的尊重。寇德卡一点也不喜欢谈论他的照片，或者坚持某种看待它们的方式，亦或是倡导某个特定的观点。然而，他“对可能向不同人讲述不同故事的画面”感兴趣，也对其他人能从他的影像中发现什么感兴趣。", Francesca）、透视问题、平衡、分量和形式，以及空间是如何被分割的时，我了解到了这一点。看看寇德卡照片中人们的面孔；看看他对姿态的刻画，对那些勇敢的捷克斯洛伐克人在试图抵抗入侵时的神情的呈现，以及这些拍摄于转瞬之间且冒着巨大风险的照片是如何被如此精妙构图的。这些都不是偶然的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "约瑟夫·寇德卡：和今天一样：做我想做的事。捷克斯洛伐克当时没有政治自由。我在工作中找到了我的自由。我曾是一名航空工程师，同时也在拍照。我热爱飞机，就像我热爱相机一样，但在1967年我辞去了工作，因为我意识到作为一名工程师我已没有太大成长空间，而我想在摄影上尽量走得更远。为了获得辞职并成为一名摄影师的许可，我需要正式加入捷克斯洛伐克艺术家协会，这很困难，但我于1965年成功加入了。我已经在1962年开始拍摄吉普赛人和剧院，并在布拉格入侵前后继续拍摄这些主题。我总是同时关注许多事情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/PAR65550.jpg", "alt": "罗马尼亚。1968年。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/PAR65744.jpg", "alt": "捷克斯洛伐克。斯特拉日尼采。1966年。吉普赛音乐节。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：是什么吸引你去拍摄吉普赛人？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：我一直很喜欢民间音乐。我去布拉格上学时，在一个乐队里拉小提琴和吹风笛。我们常在传统民间音乐节上演出。在那里，我遇到了吉普赛音乐家并认识了他们。也就是从那时起，我开始拍摄吉普赛人。我想，我对民间音乐的兴趣在拍照时帮了忙。在走访他们的定居点时，我经常录下吉普赛歌曲。吉普赛人很擅长看穿人心：他们大概明白，既然我喜欢他们的歌，那我一定还喜欢别的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "要不是1963年偶然得到了运抵捷克斯洛伐克的首批25毫米广角镜头之一，我绝不可能用那样的方式拍摄吉普赛人。这枚镜头改变了我的视界。我的眼睛、我的视野变成了广角。它使我能够在吉普赛人居住的狭小空间里工作，帮我把本质与非本质剥离开来，并在光线不佳的情况下拍出我一直想要的全部景深。通过理解并尊重其正确使用的规则，它决定了构图。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：你的戏剧摄影呢？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：1965年奥托马尔·克赖恰（Otomar Krejča）创立“门后剧院”（Theater Beyond the Gate）时，他问我想不想和他合作。我答应的条件之一是，在拍照时我可以在舞台上的演员中间自由移动。我希望能够直接在舞台上对演员之间的情境做出反应，以拍摄剧外生活的方式拍摄演出。我希望在戏剧的人为造作中触及某种真实。通过这种方式与克赖恰合作，我学会了将世界视为戏剧。然而，拍摄世界的戏剧更让我感兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PAR339722-scaled.jpg", "alt": "捷克斯洛伐克。布拉格。1968年8月。华沙条约组织军队入侵布拉格。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PAR339747-scaled.jpg", "alt": "捷克斯洛伐克。布拉格。1968年8月。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：你当时对纪实摄影有概念吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：1968年时，我对纪实摄影一无所知。我没看过《生活》杂志，也没看过《巴黎竞赛画报》。当我拍摄苏联入侵时，我是为了自己而拍的。我当时没考虑过摄影专题，也没想过要出版。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：我读到过伊恩·贝里（Ian Berry）的一段精彩引述，据我所知，他当时是布拉格那周唯一的西方摄影师。他说：“我见到的唯一另一个摄影师是个彻头彻尾的疯子，他的脖子上挂着几台用绳子系着的复古相机，肩膀上扛着一个纸板箱，居然就直接走到俄国人跟前，爬上他们的坦克并公开拍照。他得到了人群的支持，每当俄国人试图抢走他的胶卷时，人群就会涌上来把他围在中间。我觉得这家伙要么是周围最勇敢的人，要么就是周围最大的疯子。”约瑟夫，显然这个勇敢的疯子就是你。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：那一定是个危险的局势，但我当时没感觉。对我来说，真正有勇气的人是莫斯科的那七个人——在千百万人中仅有的那几个——他们在红场针对入侵进行了那周的抗议，明知自己会被捕并入狱。我认为那个时期发生的事情比我宏大得多，比我们所有人都要宏大得多。这场入侵是一场悲剧，但既然它已经发生，我很高兴自己当时在那里见证并拍摄了它。入侵期间，我拍了照片，但没有冲洗。根本没时间。我是后来才处理所有的底片的。我把一些照片留给了摄影史学家安娜·法罗娃（Anna Fárová）。她把这些照片展示给包括瓦茨拉夫·哈维尔（Václav Havel）在内的各种人看。他提出把照片带到美国去——他曾应阿瑟·米勒（Arthur Miller）的邀请去那里——但后来他不被允许成行。几张照片最终由华盛顿史密森尼学会（Smithsonian Institution）摄影部馆长尤金·奥斯特洛夫（Eugene Ostroff）带出了国。法罗娃把照片给过他看。奥斯特洛夫把照片拿给他的朋友艾略特·厄维特（Elliott Erwitt）看，后者当时是玛格南图片社（Magnum Photos）的社长。厄维特想知道除了他看过的那些之外还有没有别的照片，以及我是否愿意把底片寄给玛格南。我对此不太热心——因为我以前丢过底片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PAR339724-scaled.jpg", "alt": "捷克斯洛伐克。布拉格。1968年8月。华沙条约组织军队入侵布拉格。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PAR339742-scaled.jpg", "alt": "捷克斯洛伐克。布拉格。1968年8月。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：你之前的底片发生过什么事？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：我想在布拉格人民决定不举行示威以防给苏联占领者提供屠杀借口之后——捷克人意识到自己被算计了——单独拍摄瓦茨拉夫广场（Wenceslas Square）上的苏联坦克和士兵。在我拍的那张带着手表的手的照片里，你看不到苏联人……我爬上其中一栋建筑的顶楼，苏联人看见了我。他们以为我是狙击手，开始追我。我穿过走廊跑进另一栋楼，偶然发现我的一个朋友住在那里。我把我那天拍的所有胶卷——大约二十卷——留给了他，以防我离开大楼时被苏联人抓住。第二天我回去取胶卷，但他已经把这些胶卷交给了某人，打算带到维也纳的自由欧洲电台（Radio Free Europe）。我想杀了他。所以当局势平息后，大约在入侵两周后，趁我手里还有护照（我刚刚在布拉格之春期间第一次拿到护照），我和这家伙一起去了维也纳。我想把我的胶卷拿回来。自由欧洲电台已经把五卷胶卷寄到了他们在慕尼黑的办公室。我们被告知他们对这些素材不感兴趣。我很高兴能拿回剩下的胶卷并把它们带回了布拉格，但我再也没能拿回那另外五卷胶卷。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不管怎样，回到后来玛格南的事上，最终底片安全地运出了国并抵达了纽约。玛格南监督了照片的冲印和它们在全世界的分发。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我碰巧在1969年8月身在伦敦，当时我正随一个剧团进行拍摄。我们在一个星期日早晨（苏联入侵一周年纪念日）外出，有人买了一份《星期日泰晤士报》，上面登了我的照片。那是第一次看到我的照片被发表。为了保护我和我的家人，这些照片署名为“一个未具名的捷克摄影师”，马格南为了内部使用，仅在我的照片背面盖上了“P.P.”—即“布拉格摄影师”（Prague Photographer）的印章。随后，我匿名获得了罗伯特·卡帕金奖，这一消息在“美国之音”广播电台播出了。布拉格的很多人在信号未被屏蔽时都收听了该广播，我的一些朋友开始问我这些照片是不是我拍的。我开始担心捷克秘密警察会发现我就是这些照片的作者。马格南通过邀请我去西欧拍摄罗姆人，为我安排了在1970年离开布拉格的许可，随后我在英国获得了庇护。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0585/5399/1302/files/KOUDELKAINVASIONjacket7-22-26.jpg?v=1785357295", "alt": "约瑟夫·寇德卡：《布拉格入侵 68》", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "约瑟夫·寇德卡：《布拉格入侵 68》", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《布拉格入侵 68》现已推出精装版，它重新展现了寇德卡作品的生命力与先见之明，定格了面对政治压制时的公众反抗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：这组作品既记录又见证了苏联对布拉格的入侵。你认为它具有证据性质吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：是的——正因如此，苏联和捷克斯洛伐克政府才对这些照片的存在感到非常不满。这些照片是曾经发生过的事情的铁证。当我前往俄罗斯时，有时会遇到当年参与占领布拉格的前军人。他们说：“我们是来解放你们的。我们是来帮助你们的。”我说：", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“听着。我认为完全不是那么回事。我看到有人被杀害。”他们说：", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“没有。我们从来……没有开枪。没有。没有。”所以我可以向他们展示我的布拉格 1968 照片并说道：“听着，这些是我的照片。我当时就在那里。”而他们不得不相信我。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：当人们最终知道你就是1968年入侵照片的作者时，你作何感想？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：当人们最终明白那些照片是我拍的时候，我其实并没有什么特别的感觉。我很高兴捷克斯洛伐克的共产党人不能说我只是因为这些照片才出名的，因为当人们发现我拍了那些照片时，我已经凭其他作品闻名了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "反抗苏联入侵的第一周是绝妙的，但它并未持久。在接下来的二十年里发生的事情则远没有那么英勇。政府变得日益压迫，毁掉了许多捷克斯洛伐克人的生活，并试图抹去关于布拉格之春和反抗的一切记忆。十年前，我在捷克共和国参加马格南关于1968年的展览。当地年轻一代中有一半以上对1968年的事件一无所知，而那些确实了解的民众大多选择了遗忘。但自那以后，很多事情都发生了改变。布拉格之春在共产主义最终倒台的过程中发挥了作用，因此这些事件的影响超出了捷克斯洛伐克的范围。捷克出版商已经订购了四千本我的书《入侵 68：布拉格》（2008年）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/josef-koudelka-invasion-prague-68-5-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "约瑟夫·寇德卡，《保卫捷克斯洛伐克广播电台大楼》，布拉格，1968年8月", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：你为什么等了四十年才出这本书？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：没有人对出版这种类型的书感兴趣。我也没有。对我来说，创作新的作品要重要得多。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：那么为什么是现在？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：同样，这一切都是偶然发生的。2007年初我在布拉格与我的出版商交谈，他问我那年冬天在做什么项目。我回答说，我想最终完成我过去四十年一直在做的下一本罗姆人书籍的样书。他说第二年将是苏联入侵四十周年，并建议我们为此出一本书。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：在构思图书的结构时，你的方式有哪些不同——例如《罗姆人》（1975年）、《流亡者》（1988年）和《布拉格入侵 68》？", "links": [{"text": "Gypsies", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/products/gypsies-2"}, {"text": "Exiles", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/products/exiles"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：多合一的《罗姆人》是一种可以被称为构建的方法的结果，因为我曾有意识地努力去涵盖生活的方方面面……", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：……也就是说，这组作品暗示了一种共同的经历，暗示了我们所有人共同分享的人类生活面貌？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：你可以这么说。当我发现有什么缺失时，我会努力去寻找并拍摄它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《流亡者》是我的编辑罗贝尔·德尔皮尔（Robert Delpire）为我们在20世纪80年代中期挑选的一组照片所取的名字，这些照片主要选自我离开捷克斯洛伐克之后拍摄的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：所以这种方法部分在于识别现有照片之间的联系，而在这个案例中，这些影像围绕着流亡的概念凝聚在一起？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：流亡意味着你必须从零开始构建你的生活。你得到了这个机会。当我离开捷克斯洛伐克时，我正在发现我周围的世界。当然，人们仍然会被某些人所吸引……", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/josef-koudelka-invasion-prague-68-9.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/josef-koudelka-invasion-prague-68-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：在我看来，构成《流亡者》的影像具有一种独特的编排。其感性似乎植根于手势与动作的分散。有时会有几个焦点——这种感觉不是线性的。因此，整本书所散发出的生命力，既不同于《罗姆人》作品的亲密感，也不同于更具纪实风格的《布拉格入侵 68》。你对《布拉格入侵 68》这本书的目标是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "寇德卡：我的目标是以其所有的复杂性呈现苏联对布拉格的入侵，在尊重事件时间顺序的同时重现那七天的氛围。我与捷克平面设计师阿列什·纳伊布尔特（Aleš Najbrt）合作。我们共同挑选了最具冲击力的照片，并构思出了该书的结构。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们决定，效果最好的横幅照片，以及在报道事件方面最重要的照片，将以跨页形式呈现；然后还会有四张照片的组合，它们相互呼应，为某个特定时刻或事件提供更多信息；接着一页跨页上会有十六张照片，它们组合在一起来更广泛地说明当时正在发生的事情。一旦我们对这个概念达成一致，就开始放置图像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里斯：在准备这本书之前，你有没有重新翻阅你的底片小样或底片？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "库德卡：是的。翻阅我档案中的所有作品和底片小样时，我发现了很多决定在这本书中使用的照片，但我没有发现任何一张照片可以加入到我一直认为最好的那些照片中。一张好照片是那种能印在你的脑海里、让你无法忘怀的照片。我的大部分书都是这样构成的。这本书的概念则不同。当我们开始把照片放入我们已确定的结构中时，这本书开始变得清晰起来。通常我工作非常慢。我需要确凿地知道编辑、编排、设计……一切……都必须是这样的——它不可能以别的方式呈现。所以我简直不敢相信《Invasion 68》只花了1年时间制作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们与3位研究这一时期的历史学家合作。我们请学者们撰写简短但信息量丰富的解释性导言，并寻找与照片直接相关的文件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PAR339743-scaled.jpg", "alt": "捷克斯洛伐克。布拉格。1968年8月。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PAR339723-scaled.jpg", "alt": "捷克斯洛伐克。布拉格。1968年8月。华约军队入侵布拉格。", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "An earlier version of this article was originally published in Aperture Conversations: 1985 to the Present (2018), and revisited on the occasion of the newly released edition of Josef Koudelka: Invasion Prague 68 (2026).", "links": [{"text": "Josef Koudelka: Invasion Prague 68", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/collections/new-in-books/products/josef-koudelka-invasion-prague-68"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That everything has happened by chance might seem an odd way to begin a discussion with a photographer whose focus, intensity, precision, and sheer will are evinced in every aspect of his being, not to mention in every project he has ever undertaken. Everybody was Czechoslovak. Nothing else mattered. Miracles were happening. People behaved like they never had before; everyone was respectful and kind to each other. I felt that everything that could happen in my life was happening during these seven days. It was an exceptional situation that brought out something exceptional from all of us.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Unrelentingly alert, Koudelka is poised “to seize these chance occasions, because they can be the most revealing.” He works with an open mind and heart, knowing intuitively when, as Arthur Miller once wrote, “attention must be paid.” His acute, almost feral instincts left him with little choice but to go immediately out on the street and start photographing when Prague was invaded by Soviet-led Warsaw Pact tanks on August 21, 1968."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/josef-koudelka-invasion-prague-68-3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/josef-koudelka-invasion-prague-68-6.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Koudelka is an unsentimental photographer who approaches his work without preconceptions, and with phenomenal energy and humanity, and whose own essence appears profoundly intertwined with a hunger for personal freedom (seemingly satiated). And consistent with this spirited way of being in the world is his respect for the freedom and individualism of others. Koudelka is not at all interested in talking about his photographs, or in insisting on a way of thinking about them, or advocating a particular point of view. He is, however, “interested in the picture that may tell different stories to different people,” and in what others ﬁnd in his images."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ultimately, it is all about seeing, and so the synergy between photography and painting, for instance, is a given for him—this I learned when I brought up Piero della Francesca, issues of perspective, balance, weight, and form, and how space is broken up. article_text:
An earlier version of this article was originally published in Aperture Conversations: 1985 to the Present (2018), and revisited on the occasion of the newly released edition of Josef Koudelka: Invasion Prague 68 (2026).

That everything has happened by chance might seem an odd way to begin a discussion with a photographer whose focus, intensity, precision, and sheer will are evinced in every aspect of his being, not to mention in every project he has ever undertaken. And yet this is where Josef Koudelka has chosen to begin our discussion of the work he did that one extraordinary week in Prague, August 1968, when “the big Soviet army invaded my country, everybody was against them, and everybody forgot who he was—if he was a Communist, if he was young, or old, if he was anti-Communist. Everybody was Czechoslovak. Nothing else mattered. Miracles were happening. People behaved like they never had before; everyone was respectful and kind to each other. I felt that everything that could happen in my life was happening during these seven days. It was an exceptional situation that brought out something exceptional from all of us.”

Unrelentingly alert, Koudelka is poised “to seize these chance occasions, because they can be the most revealing.” He works with an open mind and heart, knowing intuitively when, as Arthur Miller once wrote, “attention must be paid.” His acute, almost feral instincts left him with little choice but to go immediately out on the street and start photographing when Prague was invaded by Soviet-led Warsaw Pact tanks on August 21, 1968.

Koudelka is an unsentimental photographer who approaches his work without preconceptions, and with phenomenal energy and humanity, and whose own essence appears profoundly intertwined with a hunger for personal freedom (seemingly satiated). And consistent with this spirited way of being in the world is his respect for the freedom and individualism of others. Koudelka is not at all interested in talking about his photographs, or in insisting on a way of thinking about them, or advocating a particular point of view. He is, however, “interested in the picture that may tell different stories to different people,” and in what others ﬁnd in his images.

Ultimately, it is all about seeing, and so the synergy between photography and painting, for instance, is a given for him—this I learned when I brought up Piero della Francesca, issues of perspective, balance, weight, and form, and how space is broken up. Consider the faces of the people in Koudelka’s photographs; look at his rendering of the gestures, the expressions of the courageous Czechoslovak people as they attempt to resist invasion, and how these photographs, taken quickly and at great risk, are so exquisitely composed. None of this is by chance.

The chance in this work is that he had returned from photographing Gypsies in Romania the day before; that a friend called him up to tell him the Soviets had indeed entered Prague, so he was one of the ﬁrst to witness what was occurring; that he actually had ﬁlm; that the Soviets never took his ﬁlm; and that the work got out of Prague and was published one year later to commemorate the invasion. And so we begin . . .

Melissa Harris: Can you tell me a little bit about your life before 1968, before what became known as Prague Spring? Not just photographing, but what else was important to you, and whether or not you were political.

Josef Koudelka: No, I was not political. To be political in Czechoslovakia meant being in the Communist Party, which I was not. But in the period of ’68, everybody in the society became involved in politics. Czechoslovakia had been a country where nothing was possible, and suddenly, at that time, everything was possible, and everything was changing very quickly. However, what was happening in Czechoslovakia was not about revolution. It was about regaining freedom. It was the writers who ﬁrst started calling for more freedom, and who, in doing so, also expressed the feelings and desires of the whole society.

Harris: Milan Kundera’s speech supporting freedom of expression at the Fourth Congress of the Czechoslovak Writers’ Union in June 1967 is so powerful.

Koudelka: With the abolition of censorship, everything started to change. Seven days after the Soviet invasion in Prague, we heard that one of the key conditions in the Soviets’ agreement to remove their tanks from the streets of Prague was the reestablishment of censorship.

All suppression of opinions, including the forcible suppression of wrong opinions, is hostile to truth in its consequences. For the truth can only be reached by a dialogue of free opinions enjoying equal rights. Any interference with freedom of thought and word, however discreet the mechanics and terminology of such censorship, is a scandal in this century.

Harris: What was important to you at that time?

Koudelka: The same as today: to do what I wanted to do. There was no political freedom in Czechoslovakia. I found my freedom through doing my work. I worked as an aeronautical engineer and at the same time I was taking photographs. I loved airplanes as much as I love the camera, but in 1967 I left my job because I realized that I could not grow much more as an engineer and I wanted to try to go as far as I could in photography. In order to be permitted to quit my job and become a photographer, I needed to officially join the Czechoslovak artists’ union, which was difficult, but I succeeded in 1965. I had already started photographing Gypsies and the theater in 1962, and continued photographing these subjects before and after the invasion of Prague. I’m always looking at many things simultaneously.

Harris: What drew you to the Gypsies?

Koudelka: I’ve always loved folk music. When I went to Prague to study I played the violin and bagpipes in a group. We used to play at traditional folk festivals. There, I met Gypsy musicians and got to know them. That’s when I began to photograph Gypsies. I think my interest in folk music helped me when taking photographs. While visiting their settlements I often made recordings of Gypsy songs. Gypsies are good psychologists: they probably understood that if I liked their songs, then I must have liked something more.

I could never have photographed the Gypsies the way I did if, in 1963, I hadn’t by chance acquired one of the ﬁrst 25 mm wide-angle lenses that came to Czechoslovakia. This lens changed my vision. My eyes, my vision became wide angle. It enabled me to work in the small spaces where Gypsies lived, helped me to separate the essential from the unessential and to achieve in bad light the full depth of ﬁeld that I had always wanted. By my understanding and respecting the rules of its proper use, it determined the composition.

Harris: And what about your theater work?

Koudelka: When Otomar Krejča founded the Theater Beyond the Gate in 1965, he asked me if I wanted to work with him. One of my conditions for agreeing was that when taking photographs, I could move freely among the actors on the stage. I wanted to be able to react to situations between the actors directly onstage, photographing the performance in the same way I photographed life outside the theater. I hoped to get at something real within the artiﬁciality of the theater. By working with Krejča in this way, I learned to see the world as theater. However, to photograph the theater of the world interests me more.

Harris: Were you aware of photojournalism at the time?

Koudelka: In 1968, I knew nothing about photojournalism. I never saw Life , I never saw Paris Match . When I photographed the Soviet invasion, I did it for myself. I was not thinking about a photo-essay or publishing.

Harris: I read a great quote by Ian Berry, who I gather was the only Western photographer in Prague that week. He said: “The only other photographer I saw was an absolute maniac who had a couple of old-fashioned cameras on string round his neck and a cardboard box over his shoulders, who was actually just going up to the Russians, clambering over their tanks and photographing them openly. He had the support of the crowd, who would move in and surround him whenever the Russians tried to take his film. I felt either this guy was the bravest man around or he is the biggest lunatic around.” Apparently, Josef, this brave lunatic was you.

Koudelka: It must have been a dangerous situation but I didn’t feel it. For me, the people with real courage were those seven Russians in Moscow—the only ones out of millions—who protested that week in Red Square against the invasion, knowing they would be arrested and go to prison. I think what happened in that time was much bigger than me, much bigger than all of us. The invasion was tragic, but if it was going to happen, I’m glad I was there to witness and photograph it. During the invasion, I took photographs but didn’t develop them. There wasn’t time for that. It was only later that I processed everything. I left some photographs with the photography historian Anna Fárová. She showed them to various people, including Václav Havel. He offered to take them to America—where he had been invited by Arthur Miller—but then he was not allowed to go. Several photographs were eventually taken out of the country by Eugene Ostroff, curator of the photography department at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. Fárová had shown them to him. Ostroff showed them to his friend Elliott Erwitt, who was then president of the photo agency Magnum Photos. Erwitt wanted to know whether there were photographs other than the ones he had seen, and whether I would be willing to send the negatives to Magnum. I wasn’t too keen on that—having lost my negatives previously.

Harris: What had happened earlier with your negatives?

Koudelka: I wanted to take a photograph of the Soviet tanks and soldiers alone in Wenceslas Square after the people of Prague had decided not to demonstrate so as not to give the Soviet occupiers a pretext for a massacre—the Czechs realized they were being set up. In my photograph of the hand with the watch, you don’t see the Soviets . . . I climbed to the top of one of the buildings, and the Soviets saw me. They thought I was a sniper and started to chase me. I ran through hallways into another building, and by chance found that a friend of mine was living there. I left all the ﬁlm I had shot that day—about twenty rolls—with him, just in case the Soviets caught me when I left the building. The next day I returned to get the ﬁlm, but he had given the rolls to someone to take to Radio Free Europe in Vienna. I wanted to kill him. So when things had quieted down, about two weeks after the invasion, and while I still had my passport (which I had only just gotten for the ﬁrst time during the Prague Spring), I went with this guy to Vienna. I wanted to get my ﬁlm back. Radio Free Europe had already sent ﬁve rolls to their office in Munich. We were told they were not interested in the material. I was happy to get the rest of the rolls and I brought them back to Prague, but I never got back the ﬁve other rolls.

Anyway, to go back to what happened later with Magnum, in the end, the negatives got safely out of the country and arrived in New York. Magnum supervised the printing of the photographs and their distribution all over the world.

I happened to be in London in August 1969 with a theater group that I was photographing. We went out one Sunday morning (the first anniversary of the Soviet invasion) and someone bought a copy of the Sunday Times , and there were my pictures. That was the first time I saw the pictures published. To protect my family and me the photographs were credited to an “unknown Czech photographer,” and for its internal use, Magnum stamped the backs of my pictures simply with “P.P.”—“Prague Photographer.” Then I received the Robert Capa Gold Medal for the work—anonymously—and this was announced on the Voice of America radio station. Lots of people in Prague listened to that when it was not blocked, and some of my friends began to ask me if the pictures were mine. I started to be afraid that the Czech secret police would find out that I was the author of these pictures. Magnum arranged for me to get permission to leave Prague in 1970 by inviting me to photograph Gypsies in Western Europe, and then I was given asylum in England.

Josef Koudelka: Invasion Prague 68

Now available in a hardcover format, Invasion Prague 68 reinstates the vitality and prescience of Koudelka’s work in capturing public defiance in the face of political suppression.

Harris: This work both covers and bears witness to the Soviet invasion of Prague. Do you think of it as evidentiary?

Koudelka: Yes—which is why the Soviets and Czechoslovak government were not very happy that the pictures exist. These photographs are proof of what happened. When I go to Russia, sometimes I meet ex-soldiers who occupied Prague during that period. They say: “We came to liberate you. We came to help you.” I say:

“Listen. I think it was quite different. I saw people being killed.” They say:

“No. We never . . . no shooting. No. No.” So I can show them my Prague 1968 photographs and say: “Listen, these are my pictures. I was there.” And they have to believe me.

Harris: How did you feel when it finally became known that you are the author of the 1968 invasion photographs?

Koudelka: I didn’t really feel anything when people eventually understood I had taken those pictures. I was happy that Communists in Czechoslovakia could not say that I had only become known because of these pictures, because by the time people found out I had taken those photographs, I was already known for other work.

The ﬁrst week of the resistance to the Soviet invasion was fantastic, but it didn’t last. What happened during the next twenty years was less heroic. The government became increasingly oppressive, destroying the lives of many Czechoslovak people, and trying to eradicate any memory of the Prague Spring and the resistance. I was in the Czech Republic ten years ago for Magnum’s exhibition about 1968. More than half of the young generation there didn’t know anything about the events of 1968, and most of the population that did know chose to forget. But so much has changed since then. The Prague Spring played a role in the eventual fall of Communism, so the events had signiﬁcance beyond Czechoslovakia. The Czech publisher has ordered four thousand copies of my book Invasion 68: Prague (2008).

Harris: Why did you wait forty years to do this book?

Koudelka: Nobody was interested in publishing this type of book. I wasn’t either. For me, it was much more important to produce new work.

Harris: So why now?

Koudelka: Again, it all happened by chance. I was in Prague in early 2007 talking to my publisher, who asked me about projects I was doing that winter. I answered that I wanted to finally finish the dummy of the next Gypsies book I’ve been working on for the past forty years. He said that the following year was going to be the fortieth anniversary of the Soviet invasion, and suggested that we do a book on that.

Harris: What are some of the differences in the way you structurally conceive your books—for instance, Gypsies (1975), Exiles ( 1988), and Invasion 68 ?

Koudelka: Gypsies is the result of an approach that could be called construction, in the sense that I made a conscious effort to cover the spectrum of life . . .

Harris: . . . in the sense that this body of work suggests a common experience, aspects of human life that we all share?

Koudelka: You could say that. And when I thought there was something missing, I made an effort to ﬁnd and photograph it.

Exiles is the title that my editor, Robert Delpire, gave to a group of photographs we selected in the mid-1980s mainly from those I made after I left Czechoslovakia.

Harris: So the approach was in part about recognizing relationships among photographs that already exist, and in this case, the images cohere around the concept of exile?

Koudelka: Being exiled insists that you must build your life from scratch. You are given this opportunity. When I left Czechoslovakia, I was discovering the world around me. Of course, one is still drawn to certain people . . .

Harris: To me, the images comprising Exiles have a distinct choreography. The sensibility seems based in gesture and a dispersal of movement. At times there are several focal points— the feeling is not linear. So the book as a whole radiates a vitality that is different from both the intimacy of the Gypsies work, and the more reportage-like Invasion 68 . What were your goals with the Invasion 68 book?

Koudelka: My aim was to present the Soviet invasion of Prague in all its complexity, and to render the atmosphere of those seven days while respecting the chronology of events. I worked with the Czech graphic designer Aleš Najbrt. Together we selected the strongest photographs and came up with the structure of the book.

We decided that the best horizontal photographs, and also the most important in terms of covering the events, would spread across two pages, and then that there would also be groupings of four photographs, which would play off each other to give more information about a particular moment or event; and then there would be sixteen photographs on a spread, which together would illustrate what was happening more broadly. Once we agreed on this concept, we started to place the images.

Harris: Did you go back through your contact sheets or the negatives previous to preparing this book?

Koudelka: Yes. Looking through all the work in my archive and at my contact sheets, I found a lot of photographs that I decided to use in this book, but I didn’t discover one picture that I would add to the ones that I have always considered the best. A good picture is the one that gets in your mind that you can’t forget. Most of my books are composed that way. The concept of this book is different. As we started placing the photographs in the structure we had determined, the book began to crystallize. Normally I work very slowly. I need to be certain that the edit, the sequence, the design . . . everything . . . has to be like that—that it could not be any other way. So I cannot believe that Invasion 68 took just one year to make.

We worked with three historians who are specialists of this period. We asked the scholars to write explanatory introductions that would be short but informative and to find documents that directly relate to the photographs.

Harris: You have a lot of primary sources in the book: official statements from the Czechoslovak government, testimonials, statements made by the press, by Soviet officials, as well as articles and other documents from the period, and information drawn from The Czech Black Book , an eyewitness, documented account of the invasion of Czechoslovakia prepared by the Institute of History, Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences, in the fall of 1968.

Koudelka: At the end of the book there is also a short chronology that allows the reader to follow precisely what happened, day by day. We also structured the book so that someone can immediately find the most important information: these texts are printed on black. And we always tried to preserve the essential sequence of events, although I could not always be certain of the chronology by looking at my contact sheets. Everything got mixed up when the negatives first came to Magnum in New York and they made contact sheets. Nor could I always be certain of the chronology by looking at my negatives: I photographed these pictures using a type of film that was for the cinema, which had no numbers on it.

It is for this reason that when we made the book, I wanted all available documentation to identify as closely as possible the sequence of what happened.

Harris: Invasion 68 seems unlike any book you have made before— in terms of your goals and methodology.

Koudelka: I attempt to find an approach that suits the essence of each project. I do not like to repeat myself. Repetition is not interesting after you take an idea as far as you can and get what you want to get. Otherwise repetition leads to getting stuck in your habits, which soon become rules. You get locked up in the rules and you cannot get out. So what can you do? One way is to destroy them.

Harris: To me, there seems to be a duality or tension infusing your projects. I sense always the loner, the solitary man, and yet at the same time there is often a poignant camaraderie. A feeling of tragedy permeates your work, while simultaneously it is profoundly luminous. And then, while you insist that “the most beautiful word is next ,” you are one of the most present and engaged individuals I have ever encountered, which is manifest in the intensity and emotionality of the photographs. Yet you seem to just as easily leave a subject once you’re done . . .

Koudelka: What I mean by “next” is moving, continuing, never stopping. I am not leaving anything. I was born a certain way. I think I am a visual person. I look at everything. It’s not that I suddenly drop the Gypsies, or the theater . . . I may not photograph them anymore because life has changed and I am not confronted by the same situations. But one builds on what came before.

Harris: You have spoken a lot about personal freedom and not wanting to stay in one place for too long. Do you not want to be attached to things? Is it about not wanting to be too comfortable, so that you keep experiencing freshly?

Koudelka: First of all, you have to understand who you are.

Harris: Do you?

Koudelka: I am trying.

You asked before about attachment. I don’t want to be attached to material things. I now have two places where I can work—in Paris and in Prague. Before this, I did not have a place for fifteen years. I didn’t need, nor did I want places. I have always tried to adjust my life to the way in which I wanted to live. I am now seventy years old, and so far I’ve never had a television, a car, a mobile phone, or a computer. Sometimes I will use them. I have nothing against them. But what I don’t have I don’t need.

Harris: So what matters, Josef?

Koudelka: Everything. Everything matters. Everything. Every day is a gift. Everything matters. This morning, it mattered very much that the sun came out at 8:18 am. Tomorrow it is going to matter very much, if I am here, that the sun is going to rise at 8:16 am. Everything matters. I don’t take things for granted. Everything is present for me. And if something beautiful happens, I try to enjoy and appreciate it as much as possible.

You know, we are all different. At the same time, we are all very much the same. And each of us is trying to find the way to be in this world, and there is no one way.

First published as “ Invasion 68 : Prague Photographs by Josef Koudelka,” Aperture Issue 192, Fall 2008, and republished in Aperture Conversations: 1985 to the Present (Aperture, 2018).

article_text:
On Monday, after learning the sad news of Washington Post critic Ann Hornaday ‘s death at age 66 from brain cancer, I walked out of a screening full of film critics with Thelma Adams (The Wrap). We talked about how Hornaday was a pioneering woman reviewer who raised a family, wrote well for decades with thoughtful finesse, and outlasted most of her peers, many of whom now write Substacks or work freelance. Daily newspaper film criticism is dying, we agreed.

I used to hang out with Hornaday at Cannes, or at the annual AFI Awards Lunch , where she presided over the jury. She was always lovely — and fun to be with — but beyond that I respected her criticism. I was not alone: her reviews and essays made her a Pulitzer Prize finalist in 2008.

She cared about reaching people with her writing, not talking down to them. She published the enjoyably readable “Talking Pictures: How to Watch Movies” (2017), in which she talked to filmmakers about their art, among them wordsmith Kenneth Lonergan on dialogue, Robert Altman, the master “of realism in sound,” Jack Lemmon on acting, and Spike Lee on cinematography.

In 2022 Hornaday wrote: “Of all artistic mediums, cinema occupies the trickiest space between fabrication and reality, exploiting the porous nature of both to become a third thing entirely: the distortion of the literal truth that becomes internalized as consensus history.”

One of her favorite movies, Ridley Scott’s “Thelma and Louise,” echoes one of her ongoing concerns — women. The film “had nothing to do with my real life,” she wrote in 2023, “other than the exhilaration of watching two women light out for the territory, with zero figs to give and needing only each other for support. Is this what ‘Easy Rider’ felt like to baby boomer men?”

And Hornaday supported women in her life: “She was also generous and funny and kind and would send random notes praising your work and sign them, ‘Your fan, always,'” tweeted former Washington Post writer Jada Yuan. “When she got sick, right after taking the buyout, she called because she knew I was going to film festivals and didn’t want me to worry about keeping anything secret from her friends. So, please, talk about Ann. Share your stories.”

Thanks to the Washington Post for much of the following biographical information:

Born on March 9, 1960, in Iowa City, Ann Mills Hornaday was adopted at birth by urologist William R. Hornaday Jr. and his wife, the former Mary Mills, who worked in local charities.

Hornaday was raised in Des Moines and graduated from Smith College in 1982, majoring in government. She spent two years at Ms. Magazine in New York as the personal assistant to the magazine’s co-founder and feminist activist, Gloria Steinem, who died in September.

She freelanced in New York, contributing to the New York Times, Premiere magazine, and more. She was the Austin American-Statesman’s film critic from 1995 to 1997, followed by the Baltimore Sun, before joining The Washington Post in 2002. After 23 years, Hornaday took a buyout in 2025.

She is survived by Lawrence Greenia, her husband of 26 years; their daughter, Victoria Greenia; a stepdaughter, Leila Greenia; and a brother, William Hornaday III.

Shortly before she died, Hornaday finished writing a behind-the-scenes book about the filming of Alan J. Pakula’s 1976 “All the President’s Men,” starring Robert Redford and Dustin Hoffman as the infamous Woodward and Bernstein, respectively. Hornaday had called the movie a “masterpiece” that “exemplified film as a supremely collaborative medium, with all the artists and technicians involved demonstrating superb craft, skill, taste and smarts.” The book is tentatively scheduled for release in 2028.

article_text:
È morto oggi, 16 ottobre 2026, a Roma , Enrico Lombardi , storico gallerista romano, fondatore della Galleria Lombardi . Aveva 71 anni e per quasi 50 ha lavorato tra mercato, attività espositiva e promozione culturale, accompagnando alcune delle principali vicende della pittura italiana del secondo Novecento. Le esequie si terranno lunedì 19 ottobre alle 11.30 nella Chiesa di Santa Maria in Montesanto, la Chiesa degli Artisti, in piazza del Popolo a Roma.

Nato a Roma nel 1955, Lombardi proveniva da una famiglia già attiva nel sistema dell’arte cittadino. Negli anni Sessanta il fratello Roberto aveva fondato la Galleria La Vetrata, mentre il padre Osvaldo guidava la Galleria Nuovo Vertice. Nel 1977 Enrico avviò un proprio progetto autonomo, aprendo la Galleria Lombardi nella sede di via del Babuino 70.

Dalla grafica internazionale alla pittura italiana

L’attività della galleria prese avvio soprattutto nel campo della grafica internazionale, con esposizioni dedicate a Giorgio de Chirico , Pablo Picasso e Wifredo Lam , accanto a opere di autori come Lucian Freud e dei protagonisti del Surrealismo.

Parallelamente Lombardi sviluppò un interesse sempre più marcato per la pittura italiana, costruendo rapporti con artisti come Renato Guttuso , Fausto Pirandello , Ennio Calabria e Renzo Vespignani . Dalla metà degli anni Ottanta concentrò in modo più deciso il proprio lavoro sulla Scuola Romana, sui grandi interpreti del Novecento e sulle generazioni successive. La figurazione italiana divenne così uno dei fili conduttori della sua attività, portata avanti attraverso mostre, ricerche e una relazione diretta con gli artisti.

Il ruolo nella scena culturale romana

Accanto all’attività commerciale ed espositiva, Lombardi partecipò alla vita associativa e culturale della capitale. Fu impegnato nell’ARGAM e nelle associazioni di categoria e, insieme a Luigi Martini , Enrico Crispolti , Ennio Calabria e Guido Strazza , diede vita all’associazione Roma per l’Arte.

Partecipò inoltre, in rappresentanza dell’associazione Gallerie d’Arte Nazionale, ad audizioni alla Camera dei Deputati dedicate alla regolamentazione del settore artistico. Nel novembre 2022 fu ospite dei Martedì Critici , in un incontro dedicato alla sua esperienza nel sistema dell’arte.

Il passaggio generazionale della Galleria Lombardi

Dal 2014 la direzione artistica della Galleria Lombardi è passata al figlio Lorenzo Lombardi , in continuità con la storia familiare. Nel 2015 la galleria si è trasferita nella sede di via di Monte Giordano 40, dove Enrico Lombardi ha continuato a contribuire alla definizione delle strategie espositive e ai progetti dedicati al secondo Novecento.

Negli ultimi anni aveva avviato anche una nuova fase curatoriale, lavorando tra l’altro con la Fondazione Terzo Pilastro – Internazionale. Nel 2022 seguì I favolosi anni ’60 e ’70 a Milano , presentata all’Auditorium della Conciliazione, mentre nel 2024 curò insieme al figlio Figurazione anni ’60 e ’70 ai Musei di San Salvatore in Lauro.

Sempre nel 2024 seguì La poetica della luce di Riccardo Guarneri ; tra il 2025 e il 2026 contribuì al progetto Segni dell’anima , con mostre dedicate ad Antonio Sanfilippo e Carla Accardi , e nella primavera del 2026 partecipò al progetto su Mario Schifano .

article_text:
E xactly 13 years ago this month, Tom Rhys Harries was hanging by his ankles from a meat hook every night. Playing a teenage rock’n’roll idol abducted by gangsters in a revival of Jez Butterworth’s Mojo, Harries was fresh out of drama school and the only unknown in a cast led by Ben Whishaw and Rupert Grint. The Guardian’s Michael Billington likened him to “an embryonic Elvis”.

Now the 36-year-old Cardiff-born actor has the title role in Clayface, a violent DC Comics supervillain blockbuster set in Batman’s stomping ground, Gotham City. This puts him in the company of fellow Brits in the comic-book universe, such as Tom Holland (Spider-Man), Robert Pattinson (Batman) and David Jonsson, recently announced as the new Black Panther. “I felt ready to do this,” says Harries. “Had I been younger, I’d have been suffocated by the insecurity of wanting to do a good job but not having that quiet trust in getting there.”

Harries is speaking over video call from the beach-adjacent Los Angeles home he shares with his girlfriend, Amy Allen. She is the professional musician of the two: songwriter of the year at the Grammys two years running, no less, for her work with Sabrina Carpenter and others. It is Harries, though, who is giving rock star this morning, even all this time after Mojo, in his grey denim shirt with a silver chain against tanned skin and assorted silver rings on his fingers. Stadium-rocker pomposity, however, is in short supply. Standing up to shut the door, he draws attention to his fashion faux pas. “I’ve got a smart shirt on but then these ,” he laughs, gesturing to his navy-blue shorts. “Party on the bottom, business on top. Classic Zoom.”

Harries has earned the right to relax. He spent three months auditioning to play the severely mutilated protagonist of Clayface for producers James Gunn (Guardians of the Galaxy) and Matt Reeves (The Batman). How did he stay sane all that time? “I didn’t.”

His character is rising star Matt Hagen, who has just received his first Oscar nomination when he sleeps with the girlfriend of a razor-wielding mob boss and pays the price. His face slashed to ribbons and his career in tatters, Matt’s only hope lies with scientist Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) and her miracle serum. This restores his good looks and gives him the power to change his appearance at will but comes with unstable side effects. In one scene, his eyelids melt, forcing him to snip away at the resulting sticky mess with a pair of nail scissors. Described by Harries as “the film’s tipping point of ickiness”, it is a moment that will be triggering for any conjunctivitis sufferers and plain disgusting for everyone else.

Closer to horror than anything in the superhero canon, Clayface is a cross between Darkman , in which Liam Neeson is a disfigured scientist who creates synthetic faces, and The Substance , the Demi Moore gross-out satire on ageing, vanity and celebrity. Despite being a pretty-boy actor playing a pretty-boy actor, Harries shrugs off any personal resonance in his own film about losing face. “I’m not interested in the vanity of it.” His looks, he says, “just happen to be an aspect of my work”.

A perceptive actor he may be but it is his otherworldly appearance which grabs you: penetrating eyes, a square, sinewy face, defiant chin and floppy vanilla hair. What does he see when he looks in the mirror? “I don’t know, man,” he says, squirming at the thought of analysing his own appearance. It has been integral, though, to films such as the 2016 folk horror Crow , where he exuded a Bowie-esque alien quality as a woodland-dwelling teenage mystic. “A Bowie-esque alien quality,” he muses. “You’re not the first person to say that. It’s not for me to comment on. I would hit a creative roadblock very quickly if I got too mired in aesthetics.”

Bowie was also a reference point in Harries’s first film role in 2011. Not only was Hunky Dory, starring Minnie Driver as an inspirational teacher, named after one of the singer’s albums, it also boasted a scene in which Harries leads his classmates in a mandolin-and-brass-tinged rendition of The Man Who Sold the World. Screen International singled out Harries as the cast member who “may ultimately become the star here”.

He was oblivious to the buzz. “And yet I’ve got negative reviews seared into my mind.” Proving his point, he quotes one from his early days. “It said, ‘Newcomer Tom Rhys Harries is out of his depth’. I read that and thought, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to get out of bed today’.”

The son of two teachers at Welsh-language schools, Harries has his parents to thank for being “ahead of the curve” in getting him tested for ADHD at the age of seven. “I don’t think I would be doing this job if I didn’t have ADHD. I notice traits within myself that I think are fairly commonplace with [the condition]. If I’m interested in something, I will hyper-fixate on it. That’s born out of a kind of peacefulness in being able to zero in on one thing because it gives your brain a rest.”

School was a struggle. “I was very naughty. I can really see a fork in the road where, had I not been supported by teachers and mentors, my life could have gone in a different direction.” That realisation instilled in him the need to prove himself. “It’s about repaying those people,” he says.

He “fell into” drama school, aced the audition for Hunky Dory in his first year, went from Bowie to Elvis with Mojo and has been building his career ever since: he took posh-boy roles in the horror-comedy Slaughterhouse Rulez , where he was a boarding-school bully, and the TV kidnapping whodunit Suspicion , opposite Uma Thurman. He went wild as an Ibiza DJ who meets a nasty end in the Netflix murder mystery White Lines , then joined Ralph Fiennes and Juliette Binoche in The Return , a Homer adaptation which pipped The Odyssey to the post.

Still, he has never had a showcase like Clayface. The gooey, grisly special effects may be the main attraction but the movie would count for little without his notes of rage, torment and vulnerability.

There is no escaping the fact, though, that Clayface arrives at a precarious time for any comic book movie not featuring Batman, Spider-Man or the Avengers. Box office disasters such as The Marvels , Joker: Folie à Deux and Supergirl , Clayface’s recent DC Comics stablemate which is predicted to lose more than $100m , indicate that fatigue has set in.

On this matter, Harries’s glass is half full. “That’s what excites me about Clayface,” he says. “It is trying to do something different in a space that is asking for that. The medium needs a shake-up and I hope that people feel they can support the film purely on the basis that it will allow studios the confidence to experiment.”

It seems unlikely, in the wake of the costly Tom Cruise catastrophe Digger and the recent Warner Bros-Paramount merger, that studios will be in the mood to do anything but play it safe, irrespective of whether Clayface triumphs or tanks. “Who’s to say? No one would have expected Backrooms or Obsession to come out of nowhere and do what they did. It’s such an unknown quantity.”

Time will tell if Harries is any kind of industry prognosticator but a star he undoubtedly is. Face it.

editorial_title_zh: 纽约电影节影评：《万物皆嘈杂》中，荒诞喜剧下女性奋力争取发声
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在《万物皆嘈杂》的开场镜头中，发生了许多事情，但导演尼古拉斯·佩雷达几乎不需要移动他的摄像机。它只是静静地呆在那里，凝视着窗外墨西哥城的十字路口，因为施工造成了交通堵塞。在一个长镜头中，连贯的……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《万物皆嘈杂》的开场镜头中，发生了许多事情，但导演尼古拉斯·佩雷达（Nicolás Pereda）几乎不需要移动他的摄像机。它只是静静地呆在那里，凝视着窗外墨西哥城的十字路口，因为施工造成了交通堵塞。在一个长镜头中，车辆不断聚集并堵塞路口，迫使迎面而来的司机做出危险的机动，引发阵阵鸣笛与警报声——背景音乐则是室内传来的持续大提琴音符。这种嘈杂的交响足以让楼下的新手父亲敲门，要求他的大提琴邻居特蕾（Tere，特雷西塔·桑切斯 Teresita Sanchez 饰）安静一点。她已经和另一位备受困扰的房客达成过类似的协议，但考虑到外面震耳欲聋的噪声，这个要求显得荒谬至极。正如特蕾在这部冷面、心照不宣、极简主义的伦理喜剧后续情节中所不断意识到的那样，她永远受制于其他男人的日程、偏好和选择性失聪。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "佩雷达（曾执导《拉扎罗之夜》（Lazaro at Night））是一位资深墨西哥电影人，其作品经常游走于幻想与现实之间，影片接下来的大部分时间都停留在特蕾长满植物的公寓内。无论如何，这里的活动实在太多了。在这个吵闹的早晨，特蕾将她的起居空间借给了她的朋友罗莎（Rosa，罗莎·埃斯特拉·华雷斯·巴尔加斯 Rosa Estela Juárez Vargas 饰）——另一位大提琴家兼同僚作曲家，以便她能拍摄一段关于其创作手艺的有线电视采访。当采访者拉扎罗（Lázaro，拉扎罗·G·罗德里格斯 Lázaro G. Rodríguez，佩雷达的长期合作者）和他的摄像师帕科（Paco，弗朗西斯科·巴雷罗 Francisco Barreiro）现身进行录制时，电源断了、相机的音频发生故障，隔壁的狗还叫个不停——这一系列小插曲将这次拍摄变成了一次充满诅咒的滑稽经历。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在一阵阵幽默的停顿与重启之间，两人用一些基本问题盘问罗莎，而罗莎则用简短、略显固执的回答应付着。这种僵硬的默契营造出一种令人窒息的氛围，有时看起来拉扎罗和帕科就像是在敷衍集体作业一样把问题交差了事。这给了特蕾——以及后来潜伏在房间角落的她的女儿路易莎（Luisa，路易莎·帕多 Luisa Pardo 饰）——一个插话的机会，让她得以用自己的回答（并强迫帕科给她戴上麦克风）谈论三人组在男性主导领域的工作，甚至还讲述了一个关于老鼠的气味如何影响她成为作曲家的奇幻故事。拉扎罗分不清她是在瞎编（或者至少是部分瞎编），并开始认真对待她，却没有提出任何此类爆料所应有的后续问题。他来这里只是为了收集他需要的素材。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大约在《万物皆嘈杂》进行到一半时，佩雷达加入了一些风格上的点缀，与其说是刻意宣告，不如说是悄然潜入。当拉扎罗和帕科走到室外等待恢复供电时，佩雷达依然关注着他们的对话，而镜头则留在那三位女性身上。这是一种诡异而有效的并置，就像你在没有任何视觉参照的情况下偷听一样。两人寒暄着，直到拉扎罗解释说，这场混乱的全天采访之所以可能真正有价值，仅仅是因为路易莎的父亲（也是特蕾的情人）是传奇作曲家埃斯特维斯（Estevez，何塞·罗德里格斯·洛佩斯 José Rodríguez López 饰）。归来后，拉扎罗提到了这位大师，并退缩到一个轻松的提问角度。“他对你有什么影响？”他问罗莎，仿佛房间里的任何人都没有自己的一套灵感来源。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在剩下的70分钟里，佩雷达和他的联合编剧胡安·弗朗西斯科·马尔多纳多（Juan Francisco Maldonado）沉浸在潜移默化的性别歧视之中（包括一个尴尬的场面：帕科试图为他正执导的一部电影索取路易莎的电话号码），这个片长切断了对核心复杂家庭动态进行更深入审视的机会——也就是特蕾和路易莎之间的关系，最终演变成了一场关于他们代际不安全感的充满挫败感的第三人称对话。尽管如此，从路易莎抱怨母亲在18岁时生下她并失去了独立性，或者特蕾认为女儿没有接受自己缺乏天分的事实这些争吵方式中，依然能推断出足够的内容。他们有着共同的过去、音乐天赋以及永远不会得到应有赞誉的共同理解。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "将他们绑在一起的是大家长，也就是拉扎罗无论如何似乎都更在乎的大师——当埃斯特维斯在夜间顺道拜访并完全吸引了采访者的注意力时，这一点就更加明显了。当他们在烛光下唠叨时，特蕾和路易莎听着他那份自我夸耀的成就和项目清单，以及那些永远不变的预设谈话要点。她们无法忍受这混乱一天和这种次要存在的现实，但至少可以沉溺于它的荒谬之中。“你一辈子都在做别人想让你做的事，”路易莎劝告她的母亲。“别那么在意了。”还有什么比大笑更好的方式呢？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《万物皆嘈杂》在第64届纽约电影节上展映，并将由Pragda发行。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
There’s a lot going on in the opening scene of Everything Else is Noise , but director Nicolás Pereda hardly has to move his camera. It just sits there, gazing out the window and onto a Mexico City intersection as a traffic jam forms from construction. In one long, continuous shot, vehicles accumulate and block the box, forcing oncoming drivers to make dangerous maneuvers that instigate horns and sirens—a soundtrack supplemented by the sustained notes of a cello coming from inside. The cacophony of noise is enough for a new father downstairs to knock on the door and ask his cellist neighbor, Tere (Teresita Sanchez), to quiet down. She’s already made a similar pact with another bothered tenant, but this request seems absurd considering the blaring noise outside. As Tere will be reminded throughout the rest of this wry, knowing, minimalist comedy of manners, she’s always at the mercy of other men’s schedules, preferences, and selective ears.

Pereda ( Lazaro at Night ), a veteran Mexican filmmaker whose films frequently dabble between fantasy and reality, stays inside Tere’s plant-filled apartment for the rest of the movie. There’s too much activity to leave, anyway. On this loud morning, Tere has lent her living space to her friend Rosa (Rosa Estela Juárez Vargas), another cellist and fellow composer, so she can film a cable-television interview about her craft. When the interviewer Lázaro (Lázaro G. Rodríguez, Pereda’s longtime collaborator), and his cameraman, Paco (Francisco Barreiro), show up to record, the power shuts off, the camera’s audio malfunctions, and the next-door dog won’t stop barking—among several hiccups that turn this shoot into a cursed, comical experience.

Between the humorous fits and starts, the pair interrogate Rosa with some basic questions that she entertains in short, slightly stubborn answers. The stilted rapport builds a stuffy atmosphere, and at times it seems Lázaro and Paco are mailing in their questions like a group homework project. This gives Tere—and later, her daughter Luisa (Luisa Pardo), lurking in the corner of the room—a chance to interject with her own answers (and force Paco to mic her up) about the trio’s work in a male-dominated field, even relaying a fantastical story about how the scent of rat influenced her to become a composer. Lázaro can’t tell she’s fibbing (or, at least, partially fibbing) and proceeds to take her seriously, yet asks none of the follow-up questions that such a revelation would warrant. He’s just there to collect material he needs.

About halfway through Noise , Pereda adds some stylistic flourishes that don’t announce themselves so much as sneak up on you. When Lázaro and Paco step outside, waiting for the power to return, Pereda stays keyed into their conversation while the camera remains on the three women. It’s an eerie, effective juxtaposition, like you’re eavesdropping without any visual reference. The pair exchange small talk until Lázaro explains that this messy, all-day interview might have real merit only because of the fact that Luisa’s father (and Tere’s one-time lover) is the legendary composer Estevez (José Rodríguez López). Upon their return, Lázaro brings up the maestro and recedes into an easy corner of questioning. “What was his influence on you?” he asks Rosa, as though nobody in the room might have their own source of inspiration.

Pereda and his co-writer Juan Francisco Maldonado nestle into this subtly ingrained groove of sexism (including an awkward scene in which Paco attempts to ascertain Lusia’s number for a movie he’s directing) throughout the rest of the 70 minutes, a runtime that cuts off opportunity for a deeper examination of the complicated family dynamics at its core—namely the relationship between Tere and Luisa, which boils into a frustrated third-person conversation about their generational insecurities. Still, there’s enough to infer in the way Luisa spats about her mother having her at 18 and losing her independence or Tere believing her daughter hasn’t to terms with her lack of vocation. They have history and musical gifts and a shared understanding that will never be given due credit.

What binds them is the patriarch, the maestro that Lázaro seems to care more about anyway—all the more evident when Estevez stops by at night and captures the interviewer’s full attention. As they rabble under candlelight, Tere and Luisa listen to his self-congratulatory list of accomplishments and projects and the predicted talking points that never change. They can’t handle the reality of this chaotic day and this secondary existence, but can at least indulge in its preposterousness. “You’ve spent your whole life doing what other people want,” Luisa advises her mother. “Stop caring so much.” What better way than to laugh?

Everything Else is Noise screened at the 64th New York Film Festival and will be released by Pragda.

article_text:
デフリンピック・ストーリーズ

劇場公開日： 2026年11月14日

解説・あらすじ

きこえない・きこえにくいアスリートが世界中から集まった「東京2025デフリンピック」を舞台に、デフサッカー女子日本代表とデフハンドボール男子日本代表の激闘をとらえたドキュメンタリー。 2005年に始動したデフサッカー女子日本代表は、4年後の台北デフリンピックでは世界の壁を前に無力感を味わった。その後サッカーとは別に立ち上げられたデフフットサル代表では選手たちの意識も覚醒し、2023年デフフットサルW杯でついに頂点へとのぼりつめる。4度目の挑戦となる東京デフリンピックでは、世界一を経験した監督と選手たちを中心に、サッカーでも悲願の優勝を目指す。一方、新たに立ち上げられたデフハンドボール男子日本代表には、初心者も数多く参加。彼らの挑戦はボールの投げ方から始まり、まずは初勝利を目指すことになる。 監督は、デフサッカー女子日本代表が2009年の台北デフリンピックに挑む姿を追った「アイ・コンタクト」をはじめ、知的障がい者、ろう者、電動車椅子ユーザーなどさまざまなサッカー選手たちの挑戦を記録してきた中村和彦。デフリンピックの試合模様をはじめ、選手たちの率直な想いや、競技史、社会が抱える問題などを、独自の視点と距離感で描き出す。
